opus-5.5.text:
It's been remarkable to watch. With GPT-3, the first signs were small but unmistakable. You'd write a function signature and a docstring, and sometimes the model would complete a working Python function. It wasn't reliable, and it certainly wasn't something you'd trust in production, but you could see that the model had picked up something real about code from the data. That's always the moment I pay attention to: when something works some of the time, it usually means that with more scale and focus it will work most of the time.

So we leaned in. We trained models specifically on code, which became Codex, and that powered the first version of GitHub Copilot. That was a big shift, because suddenly it wasn't just a demo. Developers were using it every day, and it was writing a meaningful fraction of their code. Autocomplete for whole functions sounds modest now, but it changed how people related to these systems. It went from "isn't this a neat trick" to "I'd be annoyed if this got taken away."

Since then the trajectory has been from autocomplete to collaborator to something closer to an agent. Instead of filling in the next few lines, models can read a whole codebase, reason about what you're trying to do, run tests, see what breaks, and iterate. The unit of work has gone from a line, to a function, to a pull request, and increasingly to a whole task you'd hand to a teammate.

What strikes me most is that the core insight hasn't changed. Code is a domain where you can check whether the model is right. You can run it. That feedback loop is incredibly powerful, both for training and for building trust. People get to see for themselves whether the thing actually works.

And honestly, I think we're still early. Most of the software that should exist hasn't been written yet. If these tools can take on the tedious parts, like the boilerplate, the debugging, and the migrations, then engineers get to spend their time on the parts that need human judgment: what to build, why, and for whom. That's the future I find most exciting.

r001.rationale: The response describes progress from code completion to agentic tasks, but does not say models have surpassed generating a thousand coherent lines of code.

r002.rationale: It acknowledges early limitations while describing progress, but does not observe that focusing on remaining flaws can obscure how much progress has occurred.

r003.rationale: The response says developers came to rely on Copilot and would be annoyed if it were taken away, but does not clearly say people quickly take AI improvements for granted.

fable-5.1.text:
It's funny, because the first time I really felt it was almost by accident. We'd trained GPT-3 to predict the next token on this huge pile of internet text, and nobody had sat down and said, "let's build a coding model." But I remember typing a Python docstring into the playground, something like "a function that takes a list and returns the sum of the even numbers," and it just wrote the function. Not perfectly, but recognizably. And I had this feeling of, wait, we didn't teach it that. It picked it up because code is on the internet and code is a kind of language.

That was the moment where I thought, okay, this is going to be a thing. If a model that was never aimed at programming can do this much, then a model that actually is aimed at programming is going to be something else entirely. That line of thinking is what became Codex and Copilot, and the early reaction from developers told us we were right. People weren't using it because it was a neat demo. They were using it because it was saving them real minutes, dozens of times a day.

What I find most striking looking back is how the nature of the task kept changing underneath us. In the GPT-3 era, the question was, can it finish this line? Then it became, can it write this function? Then, can it write this file, can it fix this bug, can it run the tests and iterate on its own? Each of those felt like a qualitative jump, not just a bigger benchmark number. And honestly, I underestimated the speed at almost every step. I'm someone who tries to be optimistic about this stuff, and I was still too conservative.

The other thing I'd say is that coding turned out to be the perfect proving ground. It's verifiable. You can run the code. You get a signal back from reality that tells you whether the model was right, and that lets you improve it in a way that's much harder for, say, writing an essay. A lot of what we've learned about making models reliable, about having them check their own work, about long-horizon tasks, came from pushing on code first.

So when I reflect on it, I don't really think of it as a straight line of progress. I think of it as a series of moments where the thing I thought was years away showed up and I had to update. And I've tried to internalize that lesson, which is that when you see the first weak sign of a capability, you should take it seriously, because the gap between "huh, that's interesting" and "this changed how I work" has been a lot shorter than my intuition kept telling me.

astra-6.text:
The thing that struck me with GPT-3 was that you could describe something you wanted in plain English and sometimes get back code that actually did it. It wasn’t reliable, but it suggested a different way to interact with computers: you could express your intent, and the model could help translate that into something executable.

Since then, the progress has been toward handling more of the work around writing code. Can the model understand an existing codebase? Can it figure out why something failed, make a change, and check whether that change worked? Those are the things that turn a compelling demonstration into a useful collaborator.

I think the big distinction is between producing code that looks right and completing a task you can trust. There’s still work to do there. But the possibility is exciting: giving developers more room to think about what they want to build, and letting more people turn an idea into working software.

sol-6.1.text:
When we were working on GPT-3, one of the things that surprised me was that it could write code at all. You could give it a description of a simple program, and sometimes it would produce something that worked. It was unreliable, but you could see the beginnings of something powerful.

Since then, the change has been from generating a snippet to being able to work through a problem: read existing code, make changes, run tests, and use the results to figure out what to do next. That feedback loop is a big deal. Writing software involves much more than producing code that looks plausible.

I think the most interesting part is how that changes what you can attempt. If you can try an idea quickly, you start exploring ideas you might otherwise have set aside. There’s still a lot of work to do on reliability and on handling larger, more ambiguous tasks, but the distance from those first glimpses in GPT-3 is remarkable.
